Facial asymmetry in photos: why it looks different from the mirror

If your face looks different in selfies and mirrors, consider the camera distance, head and neck position, lighting, and whether the photo is mirrored. A single photo cannot reliably establish the cause of facial asymmetry or whether treatment is needed.

Written by Kyung Hee Remedi Korean Medicine Clinic Published 2026-11-04 Updated 2026-11-04
In this article Photos and mirrors Four conditions that affect appearance When comparing photos What photos cannot tell you

01 · Photos and mirrors

Why do I look fine in the mirror but unfamiliar in photos?

The viewing distance, angle and lighting may differ between looking in a mirror and taking a photo. A selfie preview and the saved photo may also differ in whether they are mirrored. Before comparing the two, it is worth checking which conditions were different. [1] [2] [3] [4]

For example, the iPhone's 'Mirror Front Camera' setting saves selfies in the same orientation as the front-camera preview. Setting names and behavior may differ on other devices or apps, so check the orientation of the preview and saved photo yourself. [4]

Mirroring alone does not increase or decrease the degree of facial asymmetry. Distinguish the orientation of the saved image from the actual condition of your face.

02 · Photographic conditions

Four conditions that change the impression of a face in photos

The sources below provide evidence that photographic conditions can affect facial proportions or impressions in images. These studies did not directly measure the degree of facial asymmetry or treatment effects.

Swipe the table sideways to see the remaining content.

Conditions to check before comparing photos
ConditionWhat may look differentWhat to check when comparing
Camera distanceAt close distances, the relative size of the nose may be exaggerated. This finding comes from a mathematical model of nasal proportions, not a diagnosis of asymmetry across the whole face. [1]Check whether the distance between your face and the camera differs substantially.
Head and neck positionExtending the neck or moving the head forward can change the appearance of the jawline and the area under the chin. This finding comes from a small study evaluating photographs of three people. [2]Check whether camera height, head direction and neck position are similar.
Lighting directionThe distribution of light and shadow and the overall impression of the face may change. However, the cited study did not find changes in every regional assessment, including the cheeks and jawline. [3]Consider photos with markedly different lighting directions or brightness separately.
Left-right orientationWhen an image is mirrored, noticeable features appear on the opposite side. The iPhone allows you to set the orientation in which front-camera photos are saved. [4]Check the orientation of the preview and saved photo, and the app's mirroring settings.

03 · Comparing photos

Keep conditions similar when documenting changes

When comparing photos taken at different times, it helps to avoid mixing in differences in photographic conditions. The following are everyday recording suggestions based on the sources above; they do not replace standardized clinical photography or diagnosis.

  1. Use the same device and settings. Record whether you used the front or rear camera, whether the image was mirrored, and whether filters or retouching features were enabled.
  2. Keep distance, height and posture similar. Do not compare a photo with your chin raised or head turned to a frontal photo as though the conditions were the same.
  3. Check lighting and facial expression. Use a location with a similar direction of light, and also note your facial expression when taking the photo.
  4. Record changes beyond what appears in photos. Note when you first noticed differences and whether jaw movement or discomfort changed as well, so you can explain this during a consultation.

Even if the differences between photos are substantial, they cannot be attributed to a single photographic condition alone. Conversely, matching the conditions does not mean that photos alone can identify the cause.

04 · Limits of interpretation

Can photos alone reveal the cause of facial asymmetry?

Photos can document visible differences, but a single photo cannot readily distinguish which factors are involved, such as facial bones, soft tissue or jaw joints. Seoul National University Hospital explains that assessment is based on a consultation and clinical examination inside and outside the mouth, with additional tests as needed. [5]

References

The discussion of photographic conditions draws on original research and device-manufacturer guidance; the limits of diagnosis draw on a medical institution's health information. Distinguish photographic research findings from an assessment of your actual condition.

  1. Ward B et al. Nasal Distortion in Short-Distance Photographs: The Selfie Effect. 2018.A mathematical model studying short camera distances and the relative size of the nose.
  2. Sommer DD, Mendelsohn M. Pitfalls of nonstandardized photography in facial plastic surgery patients. 2004.A study in which 20 observers assessed photographs of three people in different positions.
  3. Hernandez CA et al. The Influence of Different Light Angles During Standardized Patient Photographic Assessment on the Aesthetic Perception of the Face. 2021.A study examining how lighting angles affected evaluations of facial photographs of 51 people.
  4. Apple. Take a selfie with your iPhone camera.Guidance on the front-camera mirroring setting. Settings may vary by device and app.
  5. Seoul National University Hospital. Facial asymmetry.Medical information on the scope of diagnosis and testing, and whether treatment is needed.
